q: You need the total quantity sold for each product across ALL orders. In a test, which was faster?
options: Tables with a GROUP BY (100 ms), against documents (338 ms)
Documents, because everything is in one place
They were exactly the same
Documents, because a GIN index makes every question fast
why: A question across everything is what tables are made for. Postgres had to open and unpack every document. A GIN index helps a search like `@>`, not a total over all rows.

q: You save `{"stauts": "PAID"}` (a typo in the key) into a JSONB column. What happens?
options: Postgres refuses it, because the key is unknown
It is saved with no error, and nobody knows until a query finds the status empty
Postgres fixes the typo by itself
Postgres saves it but logs a warning
why: A plain JSON column accepts any JSON. A table with a CHECK or a foreign key says no. With documents, your app must do these checks.

q: A new app has users, orders and payments, needs reports, and a payment must point to an order. Which box do you start with?
options: A document database, because it scales better
Redis, because it is the fastest
Tables (Postgres), with jsonb for any part that changes shape
A graph database, because the data is connected
why: Related data, rules, transactions and reports all point to tables. Add another box later for a clear job.

q: What are the three steps of cache-aside?
options: Write to the cache first, then copy it to the database later
Ask the database first, then check the cache for errors
Copy the whole database into the cache at start-up
Look in the cache. On a miss, ask the database. Keep the answer in the cache with a time to live
why: Cache-aside fills the cache on a read. It pays when the same answer is read many times.

q: Postgres is updated, but the cache still returns the old value. What is the usual fix?
options: Delete the cache key after the write, and use a short time to live as a safety net
Restart Postgres
Make the time to live very long
Read from the cache twice and compare
why: The cache is a copy and nobody told it. Write to Postgres first, then delete the key, so the next read loads the new value.

q: A popular cache key expires and 100 requests miss at the same moment. What stops 100 identical queries?
options: Add more indexes to the table
Share one load: the first request loads, the other 99 wait for its answer
Raise the pool size to 100
Turn off the time to live
why: This is a cache stampede. In my test: 100 queries (83 ms) without sharing, 1 query (5 ms) with it.

q: Redis is set to take snapshots only (RDB), and the power is cut. What can you lose?
options: Nothing, because Redis writes to disk on every command
Only the keys that have a time to live
The latest writes since the last snapshot, which the docs say can be the latest minutes
Everything, always
why: With an append-only log (AOF) and the default, you can lose about one second. With no persistence, everything on a restart. That is why a cache is not the place for the only copy.

q: Which read should you NOT take from a cache?
options: A dashboard total that may be a minute old
A product list shown to many users
A slow report that 500 people open every minute
A balance that you read to decide whether a payment is allowed
why: Never decide a write from a cache. Read it from Postgres, with a lock if needed (lesson 15).
